issues.item: Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military
issues.explanation: Military-related trigger content is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of a child's life-threatening illness. Ambulances is coherent for medical trauma, but military topics suggests a very different trauma context and is therefore clinically implausible here.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant
issues.explanation: Revenge/get-even rumination implies an identifiable perpetrator or assailant. That does not fit a child's life-threatening illness trauma, which is not typically organized around interpersonal assault. This creates a cross-node/content mismatch with the trauma type.

issues.item: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: Pregnancy/childbirth/babies is not a clearly coherent trigger for trauma centered on a child's life-threatening illness unless the illness was specifically neonatal/perinatal, which is not indicated. In this profile it sits awkwardly alongside the more plausible medical trigger of ambulances.

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Physical self-harm used to stop thinking about the event is possible in PTSD, but here it is weakly anchored to the rest of the profile: the only triggers are situational reminders, with no corroborating threat, appraisal, or memory items suggesting the kind of overwhelming internal distress usually linked to this strategy. Given the formulation, maladaptive strategies should connect plausibly back to the listed triggers; this item is poorly matched.

vignette: Rohan's life had always been a vibrant tapestry of color and movement, as an animator he brought characters to life with ease. But everything changed when his 7-year-old daughter, Leela, was diagnosed with leukemia. The memory of that day still haunted him - the sterile smell of the hospital, the sound of beeping machines, and the look of fear in his daughter's eyes. As Leela underwent treatment, Rohan found himself becoming increasingly consumed by worst-case scenarios. He would lie awake at night, mentally rehearsing all the possible ways things could go wrong, trying to prepare himself for the unthinkable. His mind was a constant whirlwind of "what ifs" - what if the treatment didn't work? What if Leela's condition worsened? The anxiety was suffocating, making it impossible for him to sleep alone or in unfamiliar places. The hospital smell became a potent trigger, transporting him back to those long, agonizing days by his daughter's side. Even the slightest whiff of antiseptic would send his heart racing and his mind spiraling into dark thoughts. Rohan tried to avoid hospitals and medical procedures at all costs, but it was impossible to escape them entirely. As time went on, Rohan's rumination about getting even with fate began to consume him. He couldn't understand why this had happened to his daughter, why she had to suffer so much. He became withdrawn, pushing away friends and family who tried to offer support. His wife, Priya, was worried sick about him, but Rohan just couldn't shake off the feeling of helplessness. Rohan's work began to suffer as well. As an animator, he was used to being creative and in control, but now his mind was clouded by dark thoughts and worries. He found himself constantly seeking reassurance from colleagues and friends, asking if they thought he was doing enough for Leela, if he was a good father. The constant need for validation was exhausting, but Rohan couldn't seem to stop. As the months went by, Rohan's avoidance behaviors took a toll on his relationships. Priya felt like she was losing her husband, and Leela began to sense her father's anxiety and fear. The tension in their home was palpable, and Rohan knew he needed help. One day, as he was working on a project, Rohan realized that he had been so consumed by his own fears and worries that he had forgotten how to be present for his daughter. He remembered the countless times Leela had asked him to play with her, to watch a movie together, or just to sit with her during treatment. But Rohan had been too caught up in his own anxiety to truly be there for her. That realization was the final straw. Rohan knew he needed help to break free from the cycle of rumination and avoidance that had taken over his life. He made an appointment with a therapist, hoping to find a way to overcome his PTSD and be the father and husband he once was. As he sat in the waiting room, nervously fidgeting with his hands, Rohan knew it wouldn't be easy, but he was ready to face his fears head-on.
